channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: AI analysis of ECG data measured by smartwatch may help detect reduced heart pumping function
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) software tasked with evaluating heart signals (ECG data) measured by smartwatches may help identify a hidden and dangerous heart condition known as left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD), although results varied between smartwatch brands and across ECG recordings, according to new, preliminary, independent late-breaking science presented today at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026. The meeting takes place Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Slow hands, quiet nights? Tai chi and a matched exercise class nudged sleep about equally in older men after cancer
item.description: Sleep disturbances affect up to 60% of people after primary cancer treatment, and they are often waved away as the price of treatment, or of age. For older men in particular, science has had little to offer. Most research on behavioral treatments for insomnia has studied women with breast cancer.

item.title: Routine invasive procedures for stable heart disease found to offer no long-term survival advantage over drug therapy
item.description: Patients with stable heart disease and abnormal stress tests who have invasive procedures early in their care do not live longer than those initially treated with drugs and lifestyle changes alone, an international study shows.

item.title: Links between early-life air pollution and lung function persist into adolescence
item.description: Air pollution can cause a wide range of adverse health effects, including COPD, asthma, low birth weight, cancer, cardiovascular disease and an increased risk of premature death. A new study from the University of Copenhagen, Danish Pediatric Asthma Center and Herlev and Gentofte Hospital shows that even small differences in exposure to air pollution during pregnancy and the first years of life are associated with poorer lung function in children and adolescents.

item.title: AI used to predict cavities
item.description: An international team of researchers is leveraging artificial intelligence to predict who is at high risk for cavities. The findings, published in the journal Caries Research, could help identify population clusters most at risk for tooth decay based on larger social determinants of health rather than on clinical diagnostics at the individual level.

item.title: Nearly 3 in 4 couples with unexplained infertility have a baby within two years of starting treatment
item.description: A new study has found nearly 3 out of 4 couples with unexplained infertility had a baby within two years of starting treatment, whether they received in vitro fertilization (IVF) or intrauterine insemination (IUI). While IVF led to faster pregnancies, long-term outcomes were similar for both treatments.

item.title: After brain surgery, man sees cat's eyes in human faces
item.description: Karl, a 28-year-old man living in the northeastern United States, has a gray tabby cat named Luna. In the morning, his cat is often the first face that he sees.

item.title: Over 9 million lives could be saved every year if countries met WHO air quality guidelines
item.description: Meeting the World Health Organization's recommended annual guidelines for air pollution resulting from fine particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide has the potential to save more than 9 million lives a year in low- and middle-income countries, say University of Cambridge researchers.

item.title: People with severe mental illness four times more likely to die early from cardiovascular disease, report warns
item.description: People living with severe mental illness are around four times more likely to die early from cardiovascular disease than the general population in England, according to a new report published today by the British Heart Foundation (BHF) with Center for Mental Health, Equally Well UK, and the Royal College of Psychiatrists.

item.title: Smoking linked to higher risk of dementia
item.description: A major review of more than 2 million people has found current smokers face a higher risk of dementia, with researchers calling for brain health to feature more prominently in antismoking campaigns.

item.title: Nonprofit hospitals' financial assistance policies often don't reflect community need, study finds
item.description: Nonprofit hospitals in communities with the greatest financial needs offer eligibility for free care similar to that offered by hospitals in less disadvantaged communities, according to a new national study from Tulane University researchers. The study, published Nov. 2 in Health Affairs, analyzed 10 years of Internal Revenue Service data from more than 1,600 nonprofit hospitals.

item.title: Cancer patients' voices could help improve care across Australia
item.description: Australians living with cancer are increasingly being asked a simple but powerful question: How are you? A study led by Flinders University and Flinders Medical Center describes how clinicians routinely listening to cancer patients about their symptoms, well-being and quality of life can transform cancer care.

item.title: Singing in a choir may improve breathing and well-being in children born with a single heart ventricle
item.description: Singing in a choir strengthens breathing capacity, decreases depression and anxiety, and improves perceived school functioning in children born with a single heart ventricle, according to a feasibility study from Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago published in Pediatric Cardiology. This intervention, including in-person and online singing and breathing instruction, was developed and trialed in collaboration with Northwestern University Bienen School of Music.

item.title: High lung pressure may protect newborns with diaphragmatic hernia from blood congestion
item.description: Brazilian research published in the journal Scientific Reports sheds light on the rapid and often fatal deterioration in the health of newborns with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). In addition to uncovering the biological mechanism behind this sudden deterioration, the study raises concerns about the treatments currently used in neonatal intensive care units.

item.title: New drug combination improves survival in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer
item.description: A new treatment approach could help people with an aggressive form of bladder cancer live longer and reduce the chances of their cancer returning or progressing, particularly those who cannot receive standard chemotherapy, according to findings from a large international clinical trial co-led by researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

item.title: Discontinuing statins generally safe for older adults without heart disease
item.description: It is generally safe for adults ages 70 and older who take statins to prevent cardiovascular disease but who have not had a heart attack or stroke to discontinue taking the cholesterol-lowering medications, according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Saturday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.

item.title: Intravenous antiplatelet therapy may improve heart function in cardiogenic shock patients compared to oral medication
item.description: Patients who survive cardiogenic shock after a heart attack are among the highest-risk patients and have a significant risk of developing heart failure. Any improvement of heart function should reduce their risk of developing heart failure in the long term.

item.title: An inside look at a molecular switch that triggers inflammation
item.description: Researchers at VIB and Ghent University have uncovered how an important driver of inflammation is activated at the molecular level. Their findings, published in Science Immunology, also explain how a medicine used to treat a severe form of psoriasis blocks this inflammatory signal.

item.title: Few meet major clinical response criteria after treatment escalation for lupus
item.description: For patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), fewer than one-quarter meet criteria for major clinical response (MCR) after treatment escalation, with Black patients less likely to meet MCR criteria than white patients, according to a study published online Nov. 2 in The Lancet Rheumatology.

item.title: New blood test claims to detect 50+ cancers before symptoms—but there's no proof it reduces cancer death risk
item.description: Cancer isn't the leading cause of death in the United States; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it's cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans.

item.title: Scientists identify inhibition of a specific enzyme as a promising target to treat pancreatic cancer
item.description: Researchers have identified a promising new target in the treatment of pancreatic cancer. A new study in The American Journal of Pathology demonstrates that blocking complement factor B (CFB), a pivotal enzyme in the alternative complement pathway, halts cancer growth and alters the tumor microenvironment. The greatest tumor suppression was observed when CFB inhibition was combined with chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

item.title: Researchers reveal how inhaled nanoplastics trigger lung inflammation
item.description: Everyday plastic products, including water bottles, disposable cups and packaging, can break down over time into tiny fragments known as nanoplastics. These particles are invisible to the naked eye and can become airborne, raising concerns about their potential to reach deep into the lungs when inhaled.

item.title: Intensive blood pressure therapy did not cut cardiovascular events in adults with diabetes
item.description: Intensive blood pressure-lowering treatment to reduce systolic pressure below 120 mm Hg in adults with type 2 diabetes, who are at increased risk of cardiovascular events, did not significantly reduce the incidence of cardiovascular death, stroke, heart attack or other cardiovascular events, compared to standard treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg.

item.title: Could a flu shot help fight skin cancer?
item.description: Injecting an ordinary flu vaccine straight into skin cancer tumors may help rally the immune system against the cancer, a small early trial suggests.

item.title: Expressive writing may help reduce negative alcohol-related consequences among people prone to heavy drinking
item.description: Writing about a drinking experience that went badly and associated feelings of guilt was linked to reduced negative alcohol-related consequences over the next year in a trial involving college students. Expressive writing may offer a fresh approach to brief alcohol interventions, which aim to motivate changes in drinking behaviors. It has been somewhat effective as a brief intervention for improving other aspects of well-being, such as emotional regulation and coping, though results for behavior change and heavy drinking have been mixed.

item.title: Starting with a statin or statin plus ezetimibe to lower LDL led to similar heart outcomes
item.description: Adults with heart or blood vessel disease who started treatment with a statin alone had rates of heart attack, stroke and other heart problems over three years similar to those who started with a statin plus ezetimibe (a nonstatin medication to help limit cholesterol absorption in the intestine) when medications were adjusted to reach an assigned goal for low-density lipoprotein (LDL), or "bad," cholesterol, according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Saturday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.

item.title: Single-pill combination helps more patients control hypertension
item.description: Antihypertensive medications combined into a single pill lowered blood pressure more effectively than typical treatment with multiple pills for patients in Jamaica and Colombia, a study co-led by UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers shows.

item.title: FDA-approved drug kills cancer cells in lab by disrupting cellular recycling
item.description: Researchers from VCU Massey Comprehensive Cancer Center recently demonstrated that the inhibition of glucosylceramide synthase (GCS) can cause death in cancer cells that is independent of changes in pro-death ceramide levels. The findings, which were recently published in Cell Death Discovery, showed that using eliglustat, an FDA-approved drug, induced cell death in several cancer cell lines. Additionally, the findings demonstrated, for the first time, that GCS and its products had a pro-survival role in cancer cells.

item.title: Doxycycline use in early pregnancy associated with higher risk of pregnancy loss
item.description: A retrospective, active-comparator cohort study found that doxycycline use for respiratory tract infections or acne during early pregnancy was associated with an increased risk for pregnancy loss. Given the frequent use of doxycycline by women of childbearing age, these findings underscore the importance of both clinicians and patients weighing the benefits and risks when considering treatment with doxycycline. The findings are published in Annals of Internal Medicine.

item.title: New surface coating could help implants bond better with bone in people with diabetes
item.description: Flinders University researchers are launching an innovative surface-engineering technology that could help to raise the performance of implantable medical devices in people with diabetes and other metabolic diseases.
